name: Tunis
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Tunis: nearshore supplier diligence, banking counterparties, Tunis court and CCAT arbitration support.
hero_lede: Tunis is Tunisia's capital and business centre, home to the central bank, the stock exchange, most bank headquarters and many offshore service and manufacturing firms supplying Europe. TDSC scopes investigative consulting from Nashville for Tunis matters, working with Tunisian counsel and conservative data handling.
intro: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia and the centre of the Greater Tunis region, which spans the governorates of Tunis, Ariana, Ben Arous and Manouba. It hosts the government, the Central Bank of Tunisia, the Bourse de Tunis and its market regulator, the Conseil du Marché Financier, and the head offices of most Tunisian banks, insurers and professional firms. The Berges du Lac district concentrates corporate offices and foreign representations. The region's economy combines public administration and financial services with IT outsourcing, call centres serving French-speaking markets, textiles, pharmaceuticals and component manufacturing in industrial zones around the city, while the port of Radès and Tunis-Carthage airport connect it to Europe.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Tunis because it is where Tunisian groups are controlled and financed. A European manufacturer may source from a wholly exporting company in Ben Arous whose shareholders and related parties are not obvious; a technology client may outsource development or customer service to a Tunis provider; a lender may deal with family-controlled conglomerates spanning banking, distribution and real estate. Political and institutional changes since 2021, including the suspension of the anti-corruption authority, have increased the importance of independent checks on politically exposed persons and procurement relationships. Disputes are heard in Tunis courts or arbitrations seated in the city.

matters.title: Nearshore supplier ownership checks
matters.text: Wholly exporting manufacturers and service firms around Tunis supply European customers. We review Registre National des Entreprises extracts, published legal notices, litigation and Arabic and French media to establish who owns and manages a supplier, and identify related parties, distress or reputational concerns before contracts or acquisitions.

matters.title: IT and call centre outsourcing diligence
matters.text: Tunis hosts many software development and customer contact providers serving French-speaking markets. We verify the provider's legal identity, owners, group structure and history of disputes, and test claims about clients and capacity, helping clients assess data transfer, continuity and integrity risks before outsourcing.

matters.title: Family group and conglomerate mapping
matters.text: Major Tunisian business groups based in the capital combine banking, distribution, industry and real estate. We map shareholdings and directorships across group companies using registry data, exchange disclosures and media, showing how control is exercised and where related-party or politically exposed connections may arise.

matters.title: Banking and financial counterparty reviews
matters.text: Tunis is the base of the Central Bank, most commercial banks and the Bourse de Tunis. We support compliance teams reviewing banks, leasing firms and intermediaries by examining ownership, regulatory decisions, published financial disclosures and adverse media, alongside the principals' backgrounds.

matters.title: Litigation and asset research support
matters.text: Creditors and litigants pursuing Tunisian parties need to know what assets exist and how they are held. We assemble corporate interests, property information obtained through local counsel and media records, supporting proceedings in Tunis courts or arbitration, with enforcement steps taken by Tunisian lawyers.

local_context.title: Courts sitting in Tunis
local_context.text: Tunis is the seat of the Court of Cassation and of the Tunis Court of Appeal, and its courts of first instance include commercial chambers that hear company and trading disputes. Proceedings are conducted in Arabic, and French-language documents generally need certified Arabic translation. Court decisions are not systematically published, so litigation history research relies on counsel, parties' disclosures and press reporting rather than open online dockets.

local_context.title: Arbitration and mediation in Tunis
local_context.text: The Centre de Conciliation et d'Arbitrage de Tunis (CCAT) is the city's established institution for commercial arbitration and conciliation, operating under the Tunisian Arbitration Code. The Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie de Tunis has also been reported as preparing its own mediation and arbitration centre. Investigative support for proceedings seated in Tunis is planned around the tribunal's procedural rules and confidentiality.

local_context.title: Registry and beneficial ownership
local_context.text: Companies register with the Registre National des Entreprises, created by Law 2018-52 and operated from Tunis, which records legal form, capital, registered office, managers and published legal notices. Beneficial ownership declarations are filed with the registry under Decree 2019-54, with access governed by a 2026 ministerial order. Property title is handled by the Conservation de la Propriété Foncière, and searches are best made through Tunisian counsel.

local_context.title: Financial supervision and data rules
local_context.text: The Central Bank of Tunisia supervises banks, and the Conseil du Marché Financier oversees the Bourse de Tunis and listed issuers, whose disclosures are a useful public source. Personal data handling is governed by Organic Law 2004-63, administered by the INPDP, which restricts transfers of personal data abroad. Investigative plans for Tunis therefore limit the personal data collected and agree transfer arrangements with counsel.

tdsc_approach: TDSC has no office in Tunis and works on Tunis matters from Nashville. We start by agreeing the purpose with the client and Tunisian counsel, whether supplier onboarding, an outsourcing decision, a counterparty review or support for litigation or CCAT arbitration. Research uses RNE extracts and legal notices, Bourse de Tunis and regulator disclosures, and Arabic and French media, supplemented by information obtained through counsel. Because we have not identified a licensing regime for private investigators in Tunisia, any local inquiries are carried out by appropriate professionals engaged through counsel. Personal data is minimised and handled with Organic Law 2004-63 in mind, including its restrictions on transfers abroad.

faqs.q: Can you identify the owners of a company registered in Tunis?
faqs.a: The Registre National des Entreprises shows legal form, capital, registered office and managers, and legal notices record changes. Beneficial ownership declarations are filed with the registry but are not openly searchable. We combine registry data, exchange disclosures, media and information obtained through Tunisian counsel to build an evidence-based view of control.

faqs.q: How do you check an IT outsourcing provider in Tunis?
faqs.a: We confirm the provider's legal identity and group structure through the RNE, research the owners and managers, review disputes and media, and test claims about clients, staff numbers and facilities through public information. We also flag data protection points, since Tunisian law restricts transfers of personal data abroad without authorisation and consent.

faqs.q: Where are commercial disputes with Tunis companies resolved?
faqs.a: Many disputes go to the commercial chambers of the Tunis courts of first instance, with appeals to the Tunis Court of Appeal and review by the Court of Cassation, all sitting in the capital. Commercial contracts may instead provide for arbitration, often through the Centre de Conciliation et d'Arbitrage de Tunis. Counsel chooses the route.

faqs.q: Are private investigators licensed in Tunisia?
faqs.a: We have not identified a statute licensing private investigators or detective agencies in Tunisia, and we do not assume that the activity is authorised as a profession. Covert surveillance and recording are constrained by data protection law. TDSC therefore scopes any local inquiries for Tunis matters with Tunisian counsel and engages appropriate professionals through them.

faqs.q: Do you work in Arabic and French for Tunis matters?
faqs.a: Yes. Registry notices, court documents and much of the press in Tunis are in Arabic, while business correspondence and many corporate documents are in French. We review sources in both languages and arrange certified translation through counsel where documents are needed for Tunisian courts or arbitral proceedings.
